title: Odin's pharm book
src: Pharmacology & Medicinal Chemistry: A College-Level Crash Course (Odin Segura, 2026), appendices: Glossary of Key Terms, Common Abbreviations, Drug-Class Quick Reference

cards.b: The movement of a drug from its site of administration into the bloodstream.
A small structural change that produces a large jump in biological activity; a warning that similarity-based predictions may fail.
The strength of binding between a drug and its target, quantified by the dissociation constant Kd (lower Kd means higher affinity).
A drug that binds a receptor and activates it, producing a response.
A ligand that binds a site distinct from the orthosteric (endogenous) site and increases or decreases the receptor’s response to the natural agonist.
A drug that binds a receptor without activating it, blocking the action of agonists.
A protein that drug designers actively seek to avoid binding, because engagement predicts harm (e.g., hERG).
A receptor for a neuron’s own transmitter that provides negative feedback on firing or release.
The fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged.
A substituent or group that replaces another while preserving key properties (size, polarity, H-bonding) and improving a liability.
The tight-junctioned capillary endothelium (with efflux pumps) that restricts drug entry into the brain.
The volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time; the body’s overall capacity to eliminate the drug.
An antagonist that binds the same site as the agonist and can be surmounted by higher agonist concentration (parallel rightward shift of the dose–response curve).
Loss of receptor responsiveness or number after prolonged agonist exposure; a mechanism of tolerance.
The reversible movement of a drug between the blood and the tissues.
The less-active and more-active enantiomers of a chiral drug, respectively.
The link between the amount of drug present and the size of the effect it produces.
The maximum effect a drug can produce once bound, reflecting how well it activates its target (intrinsic efficacy for agonists).
Non-superimposable mirror-image stereoisomers; identical scalar properties but potentially different pharmacology in chiral biological systems.
An increase (induction) or decrease (inhibition) in the amount or activity of a metabolizing enzyme, altering the clearance of other drugs.
The opposing influence of glutamate (excitation) and GABA (inhibition) that sets circuit stability; shifted by many CNS drugs.
The fraction of drug removed from blood in one pass through an eliminating organ (e.g., hepatic EH = CLH /QH).
Metabolism of an orally absorbed drug by the gut wall and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation.
The time for plasma concentration to fall by half; also the timescale for approaching steady state.
A receptor for one transmitter located on a neuron that uses a different transmitter; a major motif of cross-talk.
A ligand that reduces a receptor’s constitutive (basal) activity below the level seen with no ligand.
Any molecule that binds a receptor, whether drug or endogenous signal.
Binding affinity normalized per heavy atom; used to discourage potency gained only by molecular bloat.
Beneficial (or adverse) physiologic effects arising from the meaning, ritual, and context of treatment, not from specific pharmacology alone (Chapter 15).
The enzymatic chemical modification of a drug, usually making it more water-soluble for excretion.
Harmful symptoms produced by negative expectation; the dark twin of the placebo effect.
The fraction of receptors bound by ligand at a given concentration; occupancy = C/(Kd + C).
A drug that activates a receptor but cannot produce the maximum response even when fully bound; may antagonize a full agonist.
What the drug does to the body: mechanism and effect.
The study of how genetic variation alters drug response (pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, or immune).
What the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion.
The three-dimensional pattern of features (Hbond donors/acceptors, charges, hydrophobes) required for a biological activity.
A drug interaction or physiologic state that changes a person’s metabolizer phenotype without changing genotype.
Genuine, context-caused improvement after an inert intervention, mediated by expectation and conditioning (distinct from natural history and regression to the mean).
The amount of drug needed to produce a given effect; a matter of dose, not of maximum effect.
An inactive or poorly performing precursor converted by metabolism into the active drug.
A protein (or occasionally other macromolecule) to which a drug binds to produce its effect.
A drug’s ability to act on its intended target while sparing others; the usual determinant of its side-effect profile.
A receptor reserve such that maximal tissue effect occurs at less than full occupancy; EC50 then lies below Kd .
The condition in which the rate of drug administration equals the rate of elimination, so plasma concentration is stable (reached in roughly four to five half-lives).
The map relating chemical structure changes to changes in biological activity.
A measure of drug safety: the ratio of a toxic dose to an effective dose (e.g., TD50 /ED50 or related margins).
A reduced response to a drug after repeated exposure, requiring higher doses for the same effect.
The apparent volume into which a drug distributes, relating body content to plasma concentration.
Neuromodulator signaling by diffusion through extracellular space beyond a single synapse.
clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats
vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1

cards.f: Muscarinic agonists: how do they work?
cards.b:
Activate M receptors
e.g. bethanechol, pilocarpine
Key adverse effects: Salivation, bradycardia, sweating

cards.f: Cholinesterase inhibitors: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block AChE, raise ACh
e.g. neostigmine, donepezil
Key adverse effects: Cramps, bradycardia, secretions

cards.f: Neuromuscular blockers: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block endplate NM
e.g. rocuronium, atracurium
Key adverse effects: Paralysis, apnea

Block α1
e.g. prazosin, doxazosin
Key adverse effects: Orthostatic hypotension

Central sympathoinhibition
e.g. clonidine, methyldopa
Key adverse effects: Sedation, rebound hypertension

cards.f: Adrenergic stimulants: how do they work?
cards.b:
Raise NE release
e.g. ephedrine, amphetamine
Key adverse effects: Hypertension, insomnia

Block β1
e.g. atenolol, metoprolol
Key adverse effects: Bradycardia, fatigue, bronchospasm

cards.f: ACE inhibitors: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block ACE
e.g. enalapril, lisinopril
Key adverse effects: Dry cough, hyperkalemia, angioedema

Block AT1
e.g. losartan, valsartan
Key adverse effects: Hyperkalemia, angioedema

cards.f: Ca2+-channel blockers: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block L-type Ca2+
e.g. amlodipine, verapamil
Key adverse effects: Edema, constipation

Release NO, dilate veins
e.g. nitroglycerin
Key adverse effects: Headache, hypotension

cards.f: Cardiac glycosides: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block Na+/K+-ATPase
e.g. digoxin
Key adverse effects: Arrhythmia, visual halos

cards.f: Class I agents: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block cardiac Na+
e.g. lidocaine, flecainide
Key adverse effects: Proarrhythmia

cards.f: Class III agents: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block cardiac K+
e.g. amiodarone, sotalol
Key adverse effects: QT prolongation

Block HMG-CoA reductase
e.g. atorvastatin, simvastatin
Key adverse effects: Myalgia, liver enzymes

Inhibit clotting factors
e.g. warfarin, apixaban
Key adverse effects: Bleeding

Block platelet activation
e.g. aspirin, clopidogrel
Key adverse effects: Bleeding, GI upset

cards.f: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block proximal CA
e.g. acetazolamide
Key adverse effects: Metabolic acidosis

Block distal Na+ uptake
e.g. HCTZ, chlorthalidone
Key adverse effects: Hypokalemia, hyperglycemia

cards.f: K+-sparing diuretics: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block ENaC or aldosterone
e.g. spironolactone, amiloride
Key adverse effects: Hyperkalemia

cards.f: Osmotic diuretics: how do they work?
cards.b:
Draw water osmotically
e.g. mannitol
Key adverse effects: Volume depletion

cards.f: Vaptans (ADH block): how do they work?
cards.b:
Block V2 receptor
e.g. tolvaptan
Key adverse effects: Thirst, hypernatremia

Relax airway muscle
e.g. salbutamol, salmeterol
Key adverse effects: Tremor, tachycardia

cards.f: Inhaled steroids: how do they work?
cards.b:
Suppress inflammation
e.g. budesonide, fluticasone
Key adverse effects: Oral thrush, dysphonia

cards.f: Leukotriene blockers: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block leukotrienes
e.g. montelukast
Key adverse effects: Mood or sleep changes

Inhibit PDE, block adenosine
e.g. theophylline
Key adverse effects: Arrhythmia, seizures

cards.f: Mast-cell stabilizers: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block mediator release
e.g. cromolyn
Key adverse effects: Throat irritation

cards.f: Atypical antipsychotics: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block D2 and 5-HT2A
e.g. risperidone, olanzapine
Key adverse effects: Weight gain, metabolic

cards.f: Mood stabilizers: how do they work?
cards.b:
Dampen neuronal firing
e.g. lithium, valproate
Key adverse effects: Tremor, narrow index

Raise dopamine and NE
e.g. methylphenidate
Key adverse effects: Insomnia, low appetite

cards.f: Nonstimulant ADHD agents: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block NET or activate α2
e.g. atomoxetine, guanfacine
Key adverse effects: Sedation, BP changes

Nonstimulant ADHD agents
Block NET or activate α2

Reduce excitability
e.g. valproate, lamotrigine
Key adverse effects: Sedation, rash

cards.f: Antiparkinson agents: how do they work?
cards.b:
Restore dopamine
e.g. levodopa, pramipexole
Key adverse effects: Dyskinesia, nausea

Prefer α1-GABA-A
e.g. zolpidem, eszopiclone
Key adverse effects: Complex sleep behaviors

Inhibit COX-1 and COX-2
e.g. ibuprofen, naproxen
Key adverse effects: Ulcers, renal, bleeding

cards.f: COX-2 inhibitors: how do they work?
cards.b:
Selective COX-2 block
e.g. celecoxib
Key adverse effects: Cardiovascular risk

Activate μ-opioid receptor
e.g. morphine, fentanyl, codeine
Key adverse effects: Sedation, constipation, respiratory depression

cards.f: Which drug class? morphine, fentanyl, codeine
Local anesthetics: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block neuronal Na+
e.g. lidocaine, bupivacaine
Key adverse effects: CNS and cardiac toxicity

Activate 5-HT1B/1D
e.g. sumatriptan
Key adverse effects: Chest tightness

Bind Ca2+ channel α2δ
e.g. gabapentin, pregabalin
Key adverse effects: Sedation, dizziness

Block cell-wall synthesis
e.g. amoxicillin, penicillin
Key adverse effects: Allergy, rash

Block cell-wall synthesis
e.g. ceftriaxone, cefazolin
Key adverse effects: Allergy, crossreaction

Bind wall precursor
e.g. vancomycin
Key adverse effects: Kidney injury, flushing

Block 30S ribosome
e.g. doxycycline, minocycline
Key adverse effects: Sun sensitivity, teeth

cards.f: Azole antifungals: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block ergosterol synthesis
e.g. fluconazole, itraconazole
Key adverse effects: Liver, CYP interactions

Block viral enzymes
e.g. acyclovir, oseltamivir
Key adverse effects: Renal, GI upset

Block DNA synthesis
e.g. methotrexate, 5-FU
Key adverse effects: Mucositis, marrow suppression

Intercalate DNA
e.g. doxorubicin
Key adverse effects: Cardiac toxicity

cards.f: Vinca alkaloids: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block spindle assembly
e.g. vincristine, vinblastine
Key adverse effects: Neuropathy

Stabilize microtubules
e.g. paclitaxel, docetaxel
Key adverse effects: Neuropathy, marrow suppression

cards.f: Kinase inhibitors: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block tyrosine kinases
e.g. imatinib, erlotinib
Key adverse effects: Rash, diarrhea

cards.f: Monoclonal antibodies: how do they work?
cards.b:
Target surface antigens
e.g. rituximab, trastuzumab
Key adverse effects: Infusion reactions

Broad immune suppression
e.g. prednisone, dexamethasone
Key adverse effects: Infection, Cushingoid

cards.f: Calcineurin inhibitors: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block T-cell activation
e.g. ciclosporin, tacrolimus
Key adverse effects: Kidney injury, tremor

cards.f: Purine antimetabolites: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block lymphocyte division
e.g. azathioprine, mycophenolate
Key adverse effects: Marrow suppression

cards.f: mTOR inhibitors: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block mTOR signaling
e.g. sirolimus, everolimus
Key adverse effects: Impaired healing

cards.f: TNF-α inhibitors: how do they work?
cards.b:
Neutralize TNF-α
e.g. infliximab, adalimumab
Key adverse effects: Infection, TB reactivation

cards.f: Interleukin blockers: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block IL cytokines
e.g. tocilizumab
Key adverse effects: Infection

cards.f: JAK inhibitors: how do they work?
cards.b:
Block JAK–STAT signaling
e.g. tofacitinib, baricitinib
Key adverse effects: Infection, thrombosis

Block H1 receptor
e.g. cetirizine, loratadine
Key adverse effects: Sedation (first generation)

Slow disease progression
e.g. methotrexate, leflunomide
Key adverse effects: Marrow suppression
